strengths: The core insight — replacing a single globally fused 3D memory with multiple clean per-frame local geometric memories, and treating residual cross-anchor misalignment as a learnable problem — is well-motivated, clearly articulated, and addresses a real failure mode of existing 3D-memory-based world models (SPMem, Spatia, MagicWorld).

The coverage-driven retrieval formulation is a sensible, concrete solution to selecting a compact, complementary set of anchors along a target trajectory, and is fully specified (Algorithm 1, Figure 2).

The multi-anchor weaving controller (shared joint attention over anchor tokens + pose-aware importance fusion + target pose conditioning) is a reasonable and well-described mechanism, with ablations (Table 2, Figure 5) supporting each design choice: local vs. global memory, pose-guided vs. average fusion, joint vs. separate attention.

Evaluation is relatively thorough: quantitative comparisons against seven baselines on two datasets (500 videos) under a defined partial-revisit protocol, results on two DiT backbones (CogVideoX and Wan2.2), a single-anchor (K=1) variant that isolates the conditioning design from the multi-anchor machinery, camera-controllability metrics (Table 4), and long-horizon qualitative examples on open-domain and even third-person dynamic scenes (zero-shot generalization).

The paper is generally well written and organized, with a clear update–retrieve–generate loop framing and adequate implementation details (training steps, GPUs, control injection schedule) supporting reproducibility for the main method.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation protocol is narrow: history is limited to 21 frames and the target segment replays a 49-frame portion of the same video. This is a modest 'memory' setting (few candidates, revisiting a recent trajectory) and does not stress-test very long-horizon retrieval with large memory banks; the headline long-horizon claims rest mainly on qualitative examples (Figures 6, 12), which are cherry-picked by nature.

PSNR/SSIM against ground truth for generative video models is a questionable fidelity metric (generative models can produce plausible, non-pixel-aligned content), and gaps of ~2-4 PSNR over baselines could partly reflect stylistic/blur differences; the authors do not discuss this limitation. The 'Total Quality Score' aggregation is also under-specified.

Internal inconsistencies suggest incomplete polishing: the denoising-step schedule is 80% in Appendix A.1 but 90% in Sec. 4.1; TrajCrafter is duplicated in Table 4; 'CogVideoX-I2V-5B' vs 'CogVideoX-I2V-5B' vs 'CogVideoX-12V-5B' naming inconsistencies; typo 'Retrived' in Figure 5. These are minor but numerous.

Several strong baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are reimplementations on CogVideoX; while the reimplementation details are given, reimplementation quality is a risk, and the SPMem result (below ViewCrafter) seems surprisingly weak given its published claims. SEVA, by contrast, uses its released model — backbone mismatch across the comparison table complicates interpretation.

Local point clouds are transformed into a shared world coordinate system (Sec. 3.2), so per-frame pose errors still accumulate across memories; the paper's argument that local memory 'inherently avoids' misalignment is partially undermined by this, and the paper relies on the learned controller to reconcile it without quantifying how severe residual misalignment is or how robustly it is suppressed.

Quantitative results are only on static scenes (RealEstate10K/DL3DV); dynamic-content behavior (character masking in Appendix F) is handled by a heuristic and evaluated only qualitatively. No code release is stated, which limits reproducibility of the trained controller.

Retrieval ablation (Table 3) varies only K and shows monotonic gains without a saturation point or cost analysis (compute of rendering K anchor videos per chunk and joint attention over K·La tokens is not reported).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem: cross-view misalignment in globally fused 3D memory is a genuine failure mode of current memory-augmented video world models, and the proposed remedy (per-frame local point cloud memories) is a simple, sensible design shift.

The framework is complete and coherent: coverage-driven greedy retrieval (Alg. 1), anchor-video rendering with relative-pose conditioning, and a multi-anchor weaving controller with shared attention and pose-guided fusion are all described in enough detail to understand and reimplement.

Experiments cover two backbones (CogVideoX-5B, Wan2.2-5B), seven baselines across different memory paradigms, and ablations for each major component (local vs. global memory, joint vs. separate attention, pose-guided fusion, number of retrievals K), which is appropriate evidence hygiene.
The K=1 variant of AnchorWeave serving as a controlled comparison against single-anchor baselines is a thoughtful experimental design that isolates the multi-anchor contribution.
Camera controllability is quantified separately (Table 4), where the method shows the lowest rotation/translation error, supporting the claim that pose guidance complements anchor-video guidance.
Generality is demonstrated on open-domain images and dynamic third-person scenes in a zero-shot manner, suggesting the approach is not overfit to the training distribution.
weaknesses: The headline quantitative gains over the strongest baseline are modest: SEVA achieves comparable consistency (PSNR 21.13 vs. 21.04; SSIM 0.6711 vs. 0.6739), and AnchorWeave's advantages are mainly in the aggregate VBench score and temporal metrics. The paper's framing of 'significantly improves' long-term consistency is stronger than the numbers support.

Two of the closest competitors (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are author reimplementations on a different backbone than their original versions; reimplemented baselines are frequently under-tuned, and Table 2 (global 16.31 PSNR vs. local 20.96) may partly reflect a weak global-memory implementation rather than a fundamental limitation. The claimed core insight rests heavily on this comparison.

Claims about long-horizon world consistency — the paper's central motivation — are supported only qualitatively (Figures 6, 12). There are no quantitative long-horizon metrics (e.g., loop-closure consistency, drift over 200+ frame trajectories, or even a small user study), so the long-horizon claims are under-evidenced relative to their prominence.

Scalability is unaddressed: per-frame point cloud memories grow without bound, retrieval cost over an ever-larger memory bank is not analyzed, and no compute/latency numbers are given for the retrieval-plus-rendering loop or the K-fold controller overhead.

Evidence of carelessness: TrajCrafter appears twice in Table 4, the partial-revisit protocol (21 history frames / 49 target frames from 70-frame videos) is a relatively short-horizon proxy for the long-horizon setting the paper claims to target, and no code release is mentioned, weakening reproducibility.

The contribution is best characterized as an Applied/Systems design refinement rather than a new algorithmic primitive; under that framing the evaluation is adequate, but the incremental nature (local instead of fused memory + a ControlNet-style multi-anchor controller) limits novelty relative to the dense surrounding literature.

strengths: The core insight is compelling and well-motivated: replacing a single globally fused 3D memory (which accumulates cross-view misalignment from pose/depth errors) with per-frame local point-cloud memories, and treating residual misalignment as a learnable problem in generation, is a sensible and clearly articulated reframing of the memory-conditioning paradigm for long-horizon video generation.

The paper makes a full systems contribution: local memory construction (Sec. 3.2), a coverage-driven greedy retrieval formulation with a concrete stopping criterion (Sec. 3.3, Algorithm 1), and a multi-anchor weaving controller with shared attention and pose-guided fusion (Sec. 3.4). The components are complementary and the design rationale for each (e.g., pose-aware importance weighting to suppress misaligned anchors) is convincing.

Experimental evidence is unusually thorough: comparisons against 7 baselines across two backbones (CogVideoX-5B and Wan2.2-5B), a partial-revisit protocol with GT-paired metrics, VBench perceptual metrics, camera-controllability error comparison (Table 4), ablations of every major design choice (global vs. local memory, pose-guided vs. average fusion, joint vs. separate attention, number of retrievals K), pipeline visualizations, and open-domain 241-frame long-horizon examples including zero-shot third-person character scenarios.

The K=1 variant of AnchorWeave serving as an additional control is a nice experimental design: it isolates the multi-anchor/retrieval contribution from the controller architecture and shows the architecture itself already outperforms prior single-anchor methods.

The method generalizes beyond the training distribution (open-domain images, dynamic third-person scenes, 360° rotation) with plausible qualitative results, supporting the claim that the mechanism is robust rather than overfit to static-scene data.
weaknesses: The most direct competitors for the headline claim — Context-as-Memory and SPMem — are author reimplementations on a different backbone (CogVideoX) rather than official code. Even with stated training-matched protocols, reimplemented baselines risk being under-tuned, which weakens the strongest claims in Table 1. The fair-comparison protocol is described, but the concern is inherent to this setup.

The quantitative margins over the strongest baseline (SEVA) are modest and mixed: SEVA actually has the best PSNR (21.13 vs. 21.04) and comparable SSIM; AnchorWeave's advantages are primarily in temporal/smoothness metrics and total quality score. The paper acknowledges this but the narrative of 'significantly improving' consistency is somewhat stronger than the numbers strictly warrant.

The central premise — that local point clouds are 'clean' while global fusion is misaligned — rests on the quality of TTT3R's per-frame geometry and pose estimates, which is never quantified (e.g., depth/pose error statistics, or robustness to degradation of the reconstruction model). The failure mode of the method when the 3D estimator itself is poor is not characterized.

Scalability and cost of the memory bank are not analyzed: retrieval cost as history grows (the FoV-overlap filtering is mentioned but its effectiveness/latency at very long horizons is not measured), and the inference overhead of conditioning on K=4 anchor videos (roughly 4x control-branch compute plus shared attention over K·La tokens) is not reported. This matters for the claimed 'arbitrarily long trajectories' capability.

Evaluation is limited to a partial-revisit protocol with only 21 frames of history; truly long-horizon quantitative consistency (e.g., revisiting after 100+ generated frames, or drift accumulation metrics over the update–retrieve–generate loop) is only assessed qualitatively, so quantitative support for the strongest long-horizon claims is thin.

Minor issues that should be fixed: Table 4 contains a duplicated TrajCrafter row; the consistency-score column header in Table 1 (parse) shows mislabeled/misaligned metric names, and some inconsistency exists between main text (90% of denoising steps) and appendix (80%), which slightly hurts clarity and reproducibility. No code release is mentioned, which limits reproducibility of a training-heavy system.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated insight: replacing a globally fused 3D memory (which accumulates cross-view misalignment) with multiple per-frame local point-cloud memories, and treating residual inconsistency reconciliation as a learnable problem. The diagnostic in Appendix H.1 (44.93 dB single-frame rendering vs. 16.15 dB after 45-frame fusion) convincingly substantiates this premise.

The coverage-driven retrieval formulation (visibility coverage maximization per chunk with greedy selection) is a sensible, well-specified mechanism, and the complete procedure is provided in Algorithm 1, aiding reproducibility.

Comprehensive experimental evidence: comparisons against seven baselines across two backbones (CogVideoX and Wan2.2), ablations of global vs. local memory (Table 2), pose-guided fusion, joint vs. separate attention, and number of retrievals (Table 3), plus an efficiency analysis (Table 4) and history-length scaling study (Fig. 8).

The 2400-frame explore-and-revisit stress test (Appendix H.2) is a strong addition, showing that local-memory retrieval scales gracefully where global point-cloud merging fails (OOM around frame 1120) and quantifying revisit PSNR degradation with honest attribution of causes (synthesized errors written back to memory, pose drift).

Fair-comparison effort: non-open-sourced baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are reimplemented on the same backbone with the same training data, and single-anchor baselines are given the authors' own retrieval strategy with K=1 to strengthen them.
Honest treatment of limitations and failure modes (reflective surfaces, OOD scenes, dynamic content handling), with discussion of the static-memory design assumption rather than overstating claims.
Generalization results (open-domain long-horizon examples, 360-degree panoramic consistency, zero-shot third-person character scenario) are relevant to the paper's claims about robust memory design.
weaknesses: The quantitative evaluation is limited to a partial-revisit setting with 49-frame targets on two static-scene datasets; there is no quantitative long-horizon metric in the main table, and absolute PSNR/SSIM values (~20-21 dB) indicate the task remains far from solved, so the practical impact of the gains should be interpreted with care.

Several key ablations (pose-guided fusion in Fig. 5a, joint vs. separate attention in Fig. 5b) are primarily qualitative with no quantitative numbers, weakening the evidence for two of the paper's core design claims. Reporting PSNR/SSIM for these variants would substantially strengthen the argument.

Two of the strongest memory-based baselines are author reimplementations; despite the described care, reimplementation gaps are a common source of uncertainty, and SEVA (a non-memory baseline trained/used out of its native setting) already achieves comparable consistency scores, so the margin over the best competitor is modest on some metrics.

Originality is somewhat incremental: retrieval of past frames as conditioning and 3D-based memory exist in prior work (e.g., VMem, WorldMem, Context-as-Memory, SPMem), and the architectural components (shared cross-attention, pose-conditioned weighted fusion, ControlNet-style injection) are standard; the contribution lies in the combination and the local-vs-global memory analysis rather than fundamentally new techniques.
A minor inconsistency: Table 2 reports SSIM as 53.45/67.27 while Table 1 reports SSIM in [0,1] (e.g., 0.6727), suggesting an unnormalized or mislabeled value that should be corrected.

The retrieval and controller involve several hyperparameters (chunk length D, budget K, controller layer placement, denoising-step coverage) whose sensitivity is only partially explored (only K is ablated); more guidance on robustness of these choices would help practitioners.
No code release is stated in the manuscript, which limits reproducibility of a system with many moving parts (3D estimator, retrieval, controller training).

strengths: The core observation—that globally fused 3D memories accumulate cross-view misalignment that contaminates conditioning, while per-frame local point clouds remain internally clean—is well-motivated and directly addressed by the proposed design of local memory retrieval plus a learned multi-anchor weaving controller.

The coverage-driven memory retrieval formulation (greedy visibility-coverage maximization over FoV-filtered candidates per trajectory chunk) is a sensible, clearly specified component, and the full procedure is given in the appendix (Algorithm 1).

The experimental design is reasonably thorough: two DiT backbones (CogVideoX, Wan2.2), comparisons against multiple camera-controllable and memory-based baselines, a fair single-anchor (K=1) variant that isolates the multi-anchor contribution, and ablations covering local vs. global memory, pose-guided fusion, joint vs. separate attention, and the number of retrievals.

The appendix provides useful diagnostics beyond the main results: a rendering-quality analysis of why global fusion degrades (44.93 dB single-frame vs. 16.15 dB after 45 fused frames), a 2400-frame explore-and-revisit stress test, history-length runtime scaling, dynamic-content handling via masking, and an honest failure-mode discussion (reflective surfaces, pose drift, OOD scenes) plus a limitations section.

Efficiency is quantified with a predictable K-dependent quality/cost trade-off (~2 dB PSNR for +54s and +5 GB going from K=1 to K=4), and retrieval cost is shown to scale more favorably with history length than global point-cloud merging.
weaknesses: The headline claim of significantly improved long-term scene consistency is only partially supported: on the main consistency metrics, the gains over SEVA are marginal (e.g., PSNR 21.04 vs. 21.13, SSIM 0.6739 vs. 0.6711), and the paper itself concedes 'comparable consistency scores,' with the advantage resting mainly on temporal quality metrics. The framing overstates the quantitative margin.

Both closest memory-based baselines (Context-as-Memory and SPMem) are author re-implementations rather than official code, introducing a risk of weakened baselines; this is mitigated by using the same backbone and data, but the reimplementations' quality cannot be independently verified.

The quantitative evaluation protocol (21 history frames, 49 target frames, partial revisit) is a fairly constrained synthetic setting; truly long-horizon quantitative evidence appears only in the appendix stress test, where revisit PSNR against a single initial frame is a coarse proxy and the method itself shows gradual decline past ~1K frames.

The core method is a relatively straightforward composition of existing ingredients—per-frame feedforward 3D reconstruction (TTT3R), rendered-anchor conditioning, and ControlNet-style controller blocks with added joint attention and MLP-based pose weighting—so the novelty rests mainly on the retrieval formulation and the system-level insight rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Reporting and presentation issues reduce confidence: Table 2 mixes scales (PSNR alongside SSIM multiplied by 100, e.g., '53.45'), Table 5 contains a duplicated TrajCrafter row, and Table 3's 'at most 6K retrieved frames (6, 12, and 24 for K=1, 2, 4)' is confusing and internally inconsistent.

Dynamic content is only handled by masking moving objects out of the memory, and the proposed out-of-sight dynamic memory extension is sketched but not implemented or evaluated, leaving the applicability to general world modeling limited.

Retrieval and rendering adds ~15s per segment, which is non-trivial relative to claims that retrieval 'takes only a few seconds,' and overall inference remains dominated by the backbone diffusion model with no acceleration explored.

Training scale is modest (10K videos, 10K steps), so generalization claims—while qualitatively supported on open-domain examples—are based on a relatively small training regime, and no released code is indicated, which limits reproducibility.

strengths: The core insight is well-motivated and empirically validated: the controlled rendering diagnostic in Appendix H.1 (44.93 dB for a single-frame local cloud vs. 16.15 dB after fusing 45 frames into a global cloud) directly substantiates the central claim that global 3D fusion introduces cross-view misalignment that local per-frame memories avoid. This elevates the paper beyond an engineering variant of prior memory-based world models (SPMem, Spatia, MagicWorld).

The technical design is coherent and addresses a real gap: combining coverage-driven retrieval (formulated as greedy visibility-coverage maximization with FoV filtering), a shared multi-anchor attention controller, pose-guided fusion, and explicit target-pose conditioning. Each component is individually ablated (global vs. local memory in Table 2, pose-guided fusion and joint vs. separate attention in Fig. 5, K scaling in Table 3), and the K=1 variant is provided as a matched-protocol comparison against single-anchor baselines.

The evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons against seven baselines including recent ones (SEVA, Gen3C, EPiC, Context-as-Memory), with fair re-implementations of non-open-sourced baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) on the same backbone and training data; consistency improvements hold across two backbones (CogVideoX, Wan2.2). Supplementary analyses (camera-control error in Table 5, runtime scaling in Fig. 8, 2400-frame revisit stress test in Fig. 10) strengthen the case.

The appendix includes honest failure-mode analysis (reflective surfaces, pose drift, error accumulation when synthesized frames are written into memory) and a limitations section, which is appropriate for a paper making long-horizon consistency claims.

The efficiency analysis is a useful contribution: the predictable K-based quality/cost trade-off (Table 4) and the scaling comparison showing local-memory retrieval remains stable as history grows, whereas global-point-cloud merging degrades, is directly relevant to the paper's scalability claims.
weaknesses: The quantitative long-horizon consistency evidence is comparatively weak relative to the headline claim. The main table uses a partial-revisit setting where the target segment follows the GT trajectory; the truly long-horizon evidence (2400-frame stress test, 360-degree panoramic examples) is largely in the appendix, partly qualitative, and shows revisit PSNR degrading after ~1K frames. A quantitative long-horizon consistency benchmark in the main paper would better support the 'world-consistent' framing.

Gains over the strongest baseline (SEVA) are modest on the core consistency metrics (PSNR 21.04 vs. 21.13 for SEVA; SSIM 0.6739 vs. 0.6711), with the advantage concentrated in temporal quality metrics. The paper should more carefully separate where improvements are statistically meaningful; the abstract's 'significantly improves long-term scene consistency' overstates the margin against the best baseline.

Two of the most relevant baselines (Context-as-Memory, SPMem) are author re-implementations; the fairness of these re-implementations cannot be fully verified, and small implementation differences could affect conclusions. Table 5 also contains a duplicated TrajCrafter row, and Table 2 reports 'SSIM' values (53.45/67.27) on an inconsistent scale relative to Table 1, suggesting some presentation sloppiness that should be corrected.

The framework inherits quality from a fixed pretrained 3D estimator (TTT3R) and frozen backbone; the paper does not study sensitivity to the reconstruction model or error propagation of generated (rather than GT) history frames quantitatively, even though the stress test acknowledges that synthesized errors written back to memory are a main degradation source.

Training scale is modest (10K videos, 10K steps) and training/evaluation scenes are static; dynamic-scene handling is limited to a masking heuristic sketched in the appendix. Generalization claims to open-domain and third-person gameplay rest on qualitative examples only.

No explicit statement of code release; given the method's many moving parts (retrieval, rendering, controller injection details), reproducibility depends heavily on the described hyperparameters, and the anonymized webpage only covers videos.
